newsitem.title: USA: U.S. refiners see high oil price, ample imports.
newsitem.headline: U.S. refiners see high oil price, ample imports.

text.p: U.S. refiners are facing high oil prices from latest Middle East tensions, but saturated regional markets means there are plenty of foreign crudes being offered into the U.S. Gulf, traders said Wednesday.
Exports from Asia and Canada, usually destined for California, have been sold to Gulf refiners and are currently still on offer there.
Heavy California barrels have also migrated to the Midwest on a lack of West Coast outlets, traders said.
And in spite of a tight Atlantic arbitrage, North Sea Oseberg and Troll were recently sold into the Gulf Coast, with sellers still seen for Oseberg and Brent.
"The arbitrage (trans-Atlantic) isn't exactly open but there's no shortage of supply," said a Gulf Coast trader, referring to the narrower WTI/Brent arbitrage at $1.16 a barrel on Wednesday.
The October arbitrage was at $1.40 some 10 days ago.
Traders said British Petroleum had sold its Indonesian Minas cargo to a refiner, and probably also its Attaka and Bontang crudes.
But the company was offering Canadian Koch Alberta crude, 390,000 barrels for October around WTI minus 90 cents.
West Coast traders said the original seller had requested BP to sell the cargo outside of the glutted PADD 5 region.
The West Coast, bogged down by an unusually high number of refinery outages lately, has also been filtering excess supplies to Asia, traders said.
Meanwhile, nearby Mexican and Venezuelan crude exports continue to rise steadily, keeping the taps flowing.
Differentials have steadily firmed though, signalling good refinery demand despite the influx of supplies.
A U.S. refiner last week signed a six month contract for Canadon Seco starting in Oct for WTI minus $2.00 a barrel, which includes the cost of lightering.
Vasconia was reported sold to a U.S. refiner at WTI minus $1.95 fob on Monday, and Cano Limon at WTI minus $1.55 a barrel on Tuesday, firmer than recent sales for these grades.
U.S. imports in August averaged 8.09 million barrels per day (bpd), 8.8 percent higher than the same time last year, according to the Department of Energy.
